summary:
Fire in microgravity behaves contrary to terrestrial physics: without buoyancy-driven convection, buoyant plumes vanish, leaving soot-free spherical diffusion flames, oxygen-starved zones, and undetectable low-temperature "cool flames." Terrestrial fire codes (NASA-STD-6001B) and sensors fail to predict flame spread in enclosed spacecraft cabins. 

"Flame in Freefall" transforms fragmented data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into an actionable, intelligent fire safety platform. We engineered a Multi-Output Gradient Boosting machine learning engine (R² = 0.9929) that predicts Limiting Oxygen Concentrations (LOC), flame spread velocities, and soot production indices across varying microgravity, atmospheric pressure, and ventilation profiles. 

The platform features an interactive Research Explorer covering seven PSI investigation domains (FLEX, BASS, Saffire, ACME), an SI Research Assistant for protocol queries, an AI Predictive Modeler with safety preset benchmarks (including Artemis Lunar Base 34% O₂ / 10.2 psi risk validation), and flight disaster analyses (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir). Dual-domain earth spinoffs directly enhance firefighter safety, mine ventilation, and particulate smoke detection.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work? "Flame in Freefall" is an end-to-end fire safety intelligence system that bridges decades of microgravity combustion experiments with predictive machine learning and interactive research tools:
  • AI Predictive Modeler: A trained Multi-Output Gradient Boosting Regressor (scikit-learn) trained on 1,392 experimental data points derived from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations. It models non-linear interactions between oxygen concentration (14–100%), chamber pressure (4.3–14.7 psi), low-velocity forced airflow (0–35 cm/s), material thickness (1–10 mm), and gravity (0g to 1g). It outputs Limiting Oxygen Concentration (LOC), flame spread rate (mm/s), soot yield index, and a calibrated 0–100 fire hazard score.
  • PSI Research Explorer: A dynamic multi-category catalog covering 7 research areas (solid flammability, droplet extinguishment, advanced electric-field suppression, cool flames, soot formation, and spacecraft-scale fire dynamics).
  • SI Research Assistant: An interactive knowledge assistant grounding user questions in verified NASA technical standards and flight experiment protocols.
  • Flight History & Terrestrial Spinoffs: Quantitative retrospectives of Apollo 1, Apollo 13, and Mir 1997 fire events, coupled with dual-domain earth applications (PBI/Kevlar bunker gear, laser-discriminated smoke sensors, low-emission engine combustors).
  1. What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?
  • Crew & Habitat Safety for Artemis & Mars: Enables mission architects to test hazardous atmosphere transitions (such as the Artemis 34% O2 / 10.2 psi habitat baseline) and immediately detect critical ignition conditions before hardware integration.
  • Terrestrial Life Safety: Translates 0g droplet and soot chemistry into cleaner combustion engines, and adapts microgravity particulate sensors to eliminate false alarms in underground subways, aircraft cargo bays, and mining tunnels.
  • Accessible Open Science: Consolidates technical reports across BASS, FLEX, and Saffire into a sub-millisecond, web-accessible interface available to researchers worldwide.
  1. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?
  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, Lucide Icons, Canvas-based interactive risk gauges, responsive CSS Grid.
  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Scikit-learn (MultiOutputRegressor with GradientBoostingRegressor), NumPy.
  • DevOps & Architecture: Docker containerization, Nginx reverse proxy with SSL, fully optimized for constrained low-spec hardware (Intel Pentium dual-core architecture, 3 GB DDR3 RAM allocation).
  • Data Engineering: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data extraction and physics-informed parameter interpolation.
  1. How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider? Rather than creating another static dashboard, we addressed the core physics paradox: on Earth, hot buoyant air rises and naturally vents oxygen into the flame base; in space, lack of buoyancy means fire suffocates in its own combustion products unless cabin ventilation fans supply air, creating an invisible, spherical hazard. Our platform models this ventilation-fire coupling directly. We also placed heavy emphasis on edge-compute efficiency, proving that complex safety intelligence can execute in sub-millisecond cycles without requiring costly cloud GPU clusters.
